summary: Page 2 'Neighborhood News' feature by Nancy R. Peck, 'Big, small issues filled tiny 1882 newspaper,' profiling Alfred P. Smith of Saddle River, described as a descendant of slaves, who single-handedly wrote, edited, and printed The Landscape — A Country Newspaper (predecessor: A.P. Smith's Paper), purportedly the nation's smallest newspaper (6x8 inch pages), published for 20 years from 1882 until his death in 1901.

people.name: Alfred P. Smith

people.name: Nancy R. Peck
people.role: Byline author of the feature article

people.name: Mary Ackerman McMahon
people.role: Of River Edge; recalled her grandfather was among Smith's friends

people.name: Reginald McMahon
people.role: Provided additional source material for the article

people.name: Mrs. Peter Perry
people.role: Advertised dressmaking skills in the paper (unrelated local ad)

places: East Allendale Ave. and Chestnut Ridge Rd., Saddle River (Smith's home)

incidents.what: First issue of The Landscape (originally A.P. Smith's Paper) published by Alfred P. Smith
Alfred P. Smith died at age 65 (article states four years before his death in 1901, and elsewhere age 65); paper ceased publication after 20 years

connections: Alfred P. Smith and The Landscape are also profiled in a 1991 Record (Hackensack) retrospective as a Black civil-rights-era newspaper publisher, confirming his race and journalism career in more detail
